 Follow Us On Google Treasury Yields Rest Above 5%: How Homeowners—and Buyers—Can Take Advantage of the Moment 
 By Dina Sartore-Bodo 
 October 26, 2026 
 Realtor.com / Anthony Brown - stock.adobe.com The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield has stabilized in recent weeks, and the impact is being felt. 
 For prospective homebuyers, the rise in the bond market has led to mortgage rates crossing into the 7% range for the first time in 2026 in early October. Yet, as of this week, rates dipped for the first time in two months and the Treasury yields have paused in the 5% range.
 While concerns over mortgage rates reaching 8% have subsided, there still continues to be pressure on the market due to persistent inflation. 
 And yet, while buying a house may seem out of reach with rates so high, for those still saving for a down payment, the higher yields could present a unique opportunity to lock in a fixed rate for a longer term.
 However, whether a 10-year Treasury note is a worthwhile investment for your down payment savings depends on multiple factors, including when you’ll want to access your money and your tolerance for risk. 
 The high interest rate environment
 A constant refrain from potential homebuyers in recent years has been a desire to wait to buy until rates come down. 
 While there was a dip below 6% earlier this year, now the mortgage rates stand at 7.32% for the week ending Oct. 22, down from 7.40% the prior week, according to Freddie Mac . The decline follows seven consecutive weeks of gains that sent mortgage rates to three-year highs.
 This shift mostly comes down to Treasury yields taking a breather. The 10-year yield slipped from 5.24% to roughly 5.13% last week, largely because investors are now playing defense, watching the conflict in Iran continue to unfold, and waiting on fresh unemployment claims before making their next move.
 But what remains a “pain for borrowers,” according to Evan Mills , a financial advising analyst with Scholar Financial Advising LLC, can be an “opportunity for savers.”
 “High rates make mortgages more expensive, and it’s going to be painful to see such high mortgage rates for a lot of homebuyers, especially those who saw extremely low rates just a couple of years ago,” Mills says. “It’s going to be difficult for them to understand that this might be the new normal in this economy.
 “But that same environment makes cash more productive. Those looking to buy houses who have built up a down payment no longer have to look at the stock market for a return. They can hold that down payment in cash, in a money market, or in a high-yield savings account, and keep looking around at houses without worrying about their purchasing power decreasing.”
 As it stands, banks are offering interest rates between 3.5% to 5% on their high-yield savings and money market accounts at the moment.
 Loading... Investing in Treasurys 
 One other avenue is to invest in Treasurys directly. The higher yields have driven investors to recent Treasury auctions in droves.
 But investing in T-bills comes with a significant drawback: tying your money up. 
 “T-bills are government obligations, typically in three-, six-, and 12-month durations,” explains Mills. 
 “If you buy a $10,000 three-month T-bill, in three months you receive your $10,000 back plus the interest. You should see it as locking your money away for the duration you decide, so flexibility isn’t something you tend to get with T-bills, even though they’re shorter duration.”
 If you’re willing to commit the time, then with a 5% return, that might sound great. But let’s say the house of your dreams comes on the market next week and, given the market, the seller decides to cut the price to a palatable number. Now you have a problem. 
 “If you need the money sooner than the duration you signed up for, you have to go into the secondary market and sell it, which can be pretty volatile depending on where interest rates are at that time.”
 Still, Mills recommends them for the right person trying to save. 
 “They’re high credit quality, they have a defined maturity, and they’re fairly predictable,” he says. “You’re not nervous about credit risk, because a T-bill is backed by the full faith of the U.S. government, which is almost as sure a thing as you can get.”
 The best way to grow your down payment savings
 Timing is everything when buying a home, and if you’re still a long ways away from reaching your goal for a down payment, then accounts that require you to “lock in” for months or even years might have the greatest return right now. 
 So if you’re good to sit on the bench, you have options. 
 “Treasurys and CDs are for when you know exactly when you’ll need the money. If you have a set expense in the next six months, a T-bill that matures in six months would be fantastic,” he says
 “But if you have a down payment for a house, you’re actively looking, and you don’t know exactly when you’ll need the money, a high-yield savings account could be a fantastic place to park it for the time being.”
 Dina Sartore-Bodo is the senior editor at Realtor.com covering real estate news, personal finance trends, and interior design. She previously served as the managing editor at HollywoodLife.com, the executive editor at PerezHilton.com, and as a managing editor at Mediavine. Her work has also appeared on MSN, Yahoo News, and BlogHer. She is a proud graduate of Emerson College in Boston and is originally from New Jersey.
